newsitem.title: UK: Coffee rally spotlights low commodity stocks.
newsitem.headline: Coffee rally spotlights low commodity stocks.

text.p: An explosive rally in world coffee prices has taken futures for the arabica types traded in New York to the highest since the last big frost scare in Brazil two years ago.
Prospects of tight supply of arabicas in the Americas are cited as the reason why prices have risen by more than 50 percent since the beginning of 1997.

But leading brokerage GNI Ltd in a comment on Wednesday also blamed what it calls the "idiotic management fad" in present-day commodity markets of cutting costs by operating a hand-to-mouth buying policy based on holding low stocks.
Low petroleum industry stocks were cited in a recent "spike" in oil prices.
In the new rally in coffee, the New York futures contract for May arabicas was within striking distance of the widely watched $2 per lb mark after a session high on Tuesday at 199.50 cents.
Coffee prices last traded above $2 in 1994 when two severe frosts in Brazil led to sharply depleted world supply.
London futures for the robusta type of beans meanwhile opened Wednesday at an eight-month high of $1,760 per tonne, up $62 from Tuesday.

"You just don't have a plentiful supply of coffee right now," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka in New York. "What the market will do now is correct in the next day or two, then maybe go up again."
"You can't rule out any figure," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes, when asked if $3 coffee was on the horizon.
Ganes had predicted in January that coffee would reach $2 per pound by spring. She said then that signs of a smaller 1997/98 crop in Brazil would fuel the rally.
Since then, she says, the consensus on Brazil's upcoming crop has shifted higher but worries have surfaced about Colombian output in the current crop year.

Recently, leading US coffee brands have announced rises in wholesale prices to keep pace with the advance on futures. Price rises to the consumer were announced earlier in Germany and the Netherlands.
GNI said in its commentary on Wednesday that housewife buying was now a factor in the rise in the coffee market.
"Seriously, retail coffee price hikes have been flagged by national newspapers for two months now. As a result there has been a rush for coffee from the supermarket shelves," it said.

"The buyers have then put in orders to the roasters who have been working on...minimal stocks and a hand-to-mouth buying regime. But when the flood of orders came there was simply not the coffee to meet demand".
"This is a classic example of just-in-time inventory (stock) management of raw commodities that will be seen in a few years' time as an idiotic management fad".

Low stocks have been cited as a culprit in other recent spikes in commodity prices, notably last year on metals, oil and grain - although a drop to 20-year lows on world grain stocks resulted rather from drought than any corporate policy to cut costs.

Bumper harvests have now returned bellwether Chicago grain prices to just above $3.50 per bushel after they hit $7.50 a year ago. Crude oil shot up to $25 per barrel late last year but has now eased below $20.
Researchers at UBS Ltd in London see a correlation since mid-1995 when, they say, the petroleum industry moved to low stocks, between oil inventories and price volatility.
"The market is always affected by many factors at any point in time, but low stocks now go hand in hand with greater price volatility and higher prices", they find.
